A 96-year-old man with benign prostatic disease and dementia presented after a collapse at home. On admission, he had normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 119 g/L), a D-dimer of 1095 ng/mL, normal troponin, normal C-reactive protein, and neutrophilia (10.44 × 10^9/L). A diagnosis of venous thromboembolism was considered but excluded on the basis of Well’s score, and he was discharged with antibiotics for a presumed urinary tract infection. The next day, he returned with a swollen right knee and thigh and extensive bruising, findings that were suspicious for deep vein thrombosis. Lower limb ultrasound showed a patent venous system and identified a 45 mm popliteal artery aneurysm with an 11.4 × 5.2 cm medial leg hematoma. Seven days later, he was admitted emergently with worsening right-leg pain and difficulty walking. Examination revealed extensive bruising behind the right knee and posterior-medial thigh, a pulsatile mass extending into the mid-thigh, and a pulseless right foot without signs of acute ischemia. Repeat hemoglobin was 77 g/L. Computed tomography angiography demonstrated a 4 × 5 cm saccular popliteal artery aneurysm with a large posterior thigh collection measuring approximately 23 × 3 cm; runoff vessels were severely diseased but patent, and no other aneurysms were present.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 6×10^9/L (48% lymphocytes, 42% neutrophils), hemoglobin 85 g/L, and C-reactive protein 117. Chest radiography revealed an anterior mediastinal mass extending to the hila. CT scan confirmed multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the anterior mediastinum without other masses. The patient underwent surgical resection of the mediastinal lesions, yielding ten lymph nodes measuring 3–7 cm. Histologic sections showed effacement of nodal architecture by cohesive sheets of large pleomorphic cells with abundant cytoplasm, kidney-shaped nuclei, frequent mitoses, and occasional Reed–Sternberg–like cells. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated strong CD30 positivity in the large and Reed–Sternberg–like cells, with negativity for CD15, CD3, CD20, ALK, CD45Ro, and EMA.

A 71-year-old woman presented with a 1-week history of painful vision loss and floaters in her left eye. She had no history of myopia, ocular trauma, or surgery. Visual acuity was 20/30–2 in the right eye and 20/80 in the left eye; intraocular pressure was 21 mm Hg OD and 17 mm Hg OS. The right eye was normal except for a mild nuclear sclerotic cataract and no inflammation. The left eye had rare anterior chamber cells, 1+ vitreous cells, choroidal detachments in the nasal and temporal periphery, and an overlying retinal detachment with shifting subretinal fluid; no retinal breaks were identified. Her medical history was unremarkable. Laboratory studies (CBC, basic metabolic panel, HIV, T-spot, syphilis screen, and ANCA panel) were normal. MRI of the brain and orbits showed mild posterior scleral enhancement but no intraocular mass. Fluorescein angiography showed late leakage in the temporal periphery; fundus autofluorescence was normal; optical coherence tomography revealed shallow subretinal fluid and a posterior vitreous detachment. She was started on 80 mg oral prednisone for presumed serous retinal detachment secondary to posterior scleritis. Two weeks later, the choroidal detachments had resolved but the retinal detachment persisted and appeared more corrugated; intraocular pressures remained normal and no retinal breaks were seen.

A 63-year-old Caucasian man with a history of smoking and cardiovascular disease presented with a 1-month history of right cheek swelling. He was afebrile. Examination revealed a painless, non-erythematous, mobile, round mass (~2 cm) in the right parotid region.  
Ultrasonography showed a single lobulated, well-circumscribed, hypoechogenic cystic lesion with irregular edges and acoustic enhancement in the superficial parenchyma of the right parotid gland; a few echogenic foci suggested debris.  
Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration yielded a cystic background with “dirty” necrosis and pseudopapillary clusters of moderately atypical cells with cyanophilic cytoplasm. The specimen was classified as category V (suspicious for malignancy) by the Milan System, and salivary duct carcinoma was initially considered.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the face and thorax demonstrated a homogeneously enhancing nodular lesion in the superficial lobe of the right parotid gland, surrounded by a thin fibrous capsule, with no suspicious cervical lymph nodes or thoracic lesions.

A woman in her 30s presented with asymptomatic erythematous scaly plaques over the face and proximal extremities. The lesions started as an erythematous papule on the face, progressing to larger plaques within 10 years. There was involvement of the upper respiratory tract, causing palatal perforation and stridor, necessitating a tracheostomy a year ago. History of wheezing and breathlessness. No history of preceding trauma, fever, malaise, joint pain, cough, epistaxis, hemoptysis, or hematuria.

Multiple well-defined brown erythematous scaly plaques with central scarring measuring 2 × 1 to 8 × 7 cm on the face, arm, and thighs. Saddle nose deformity, perforation of the hard palate, and necrotic plaques on the ear with destruction of ear cartilage. Cervical lymphadenopathy: multiple, nontender, discrete nodes, ranging from 1.5 to 2 cm without surface changes. Sensory examination and peripheral nerve examination within normal limits. Respiratory examination normal.

- Laboratory Tests:
  - Hemogram: anemia (hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL)
  - Kidney function test: normal
  - Liver function test: normal
  - Fasting blood glucose: normal
  - Urinalysis: normal
  - Serologic analysis for HIV-1/2, antinuclear antibody, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies: negative

- Imaging Studies:
  - Chest radiography: normal

- Pathological Tests:
  - Punch skin biopsy:
    Image Description: Infiltrate of foamy histiocytes and pigmented yeasts without multiaxial septation (Fontana-Masson)
  - Histopathology showed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, parakeratosis, dense dermal infiltrate of histiocytes, foamy histiocytes, neutrophils, and multinucleate giant cells along with pigmented hyphae
  - Fungal skin culture: black yeastlike colonies characteristic of Exophiala spinifera species

A 41-year-old woman with a 3-year history of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis presented with the sudden onset of visual disturbances. At the time of her SSc diagnosis, she had skin sclerosis of the fingers, hands, forearms, and face, Raynaud’s phenomenon with digital ulcers, multiple facial telangiectasias, esophageal reflux, and interstitial lung disease. Nail-fold capillaroscopy showed capillary loss with dilatation and microhemorrhages. A forearm skin biopsy demonstrated increased dermal collagen and superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltration. Laboratory studies revealed a positive antinuclear antibody titer (>1:320) with a nucleolar pattern, negative anti-centromere antibody, and negative anti-Scl-70 antibody. She was treated with bosentan and aspirin, with stable pulmonary findings over two years.

Seven days before transfer, she was admitted elsewhere for fever over 38°C and headache. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed protein 161.6 mg/dL, glucose 39 mg/dL, red blood cells 0 /mm3, and white blood cells 459 /mm3 (88% polymorphonuclear cells). Serum C-reactive protein was 10.6 mg/dL and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 82 mm/h. Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated T2 hyperintense lesions in the frontal, left parietal, and left occipital lobes with leptomeningeal enhancement. Empirical ceftriaxone and vancomycin were initiated. After four days, she developed visual disturbances; repeat MRI showed increased size and number of multifocal T2 hyperintense lesions along both cerebral hemispheres and midbrain, including a 4.5-cm lesion in the right posterior lobe. Tests of CSF—including Gram stain and culture, PCR for herpes simplex virus and enteroviruses, cryptococcal antigen, and fungal cultures—were negative. She was then referred to our hospital.

On arrival, she could only count fingers at close range and also reported headache, dizziness, fever, myalgia, polyarthralgia, and bilateral foot tingling. Blood pressure was 192/103 mmHg, heart rate 48 beats/min, and temperature 37.3°C. Electrocardiogram showed sinus bradycardia. Neurologic examination revealed drowsiness, neck stiffness, symmetrical proximal and distal weakness (muscle strength 4/5), paresthesia in both feet, brisk biceps reflexes, absent patellar reflexes, and bilaterally positive Babinski signs. A 4 × 5 cm ulcer was noted over the right lateral malleolus; there was no synovitis. The white-cell count was 14,090 /mm3, C-reactive protein was 3.09 mg/dL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 56 mm/h. She continued antibiotics, and intravenous acyclovir, nicardipine, mannitol, and dexamethasone were added. Blood pressure stabilized within six hours, but her visual impairment worsened, and she developed left-sided weakness and new Raynaud’s phenomenon in her fingers. Emergent cerebral angiography revealed diffuse stenosis and a beaded pattern of the anterior and middle cerebral arteries and their branches, along with diffuse luminal narrowing and dysplastic changes in the right distal vertebral artery and basilar trunk, consistent with cerebral angiitis.
